title: gen ATLAS Looks Like Fumito Ueda’s Most Ambitious World Yet
description: Fumito Ueda’s first open-world game is not interesting because it is bigger. gen ATLAS looks compelling because it turns his oldest ideas — scale, companionship, silence and interpretation — into systems that can shape an entire world.
body:
The easiest way to describe **gen ATLAS** is to list the obvious changes. Fumito Ueda is making an open-world game. The setting is overtly science-fiction. The protagonist carries a gun. A colossal robot head can apparently become transportation, equipment, a puzzle mechanism and a companion. On paper, almost every one of those ideas sounds larger, louder and more mechanically explicit than what we associate with ICO, Shadow of the Colossus or The Last Guardian.

But that reading misses what makes the project interesting.

gen ATLAS does not look like Ueda abandoning the design language that defined his earlier work. It looks like him **reassigning its functions**. Scale is no longer only something that makes the player feel small. Companionship is no longer confined to an NPC following beside you. Empty space no longer belongs to a mostly linear or tightly directed journey. All three ideas are being pushed into the structure of an open world.

That distinction matters. Ueda has confirmed that gen ATLAS is the largest game he has made, but he has also been careful not to describe that scale in square kilometers. In a detailed [Game Informer interview](https://gameinformer.com/interview/2026/06/09/fumito-ueda-discusses-gen-atlas-details-wall-e-inspiration-and-why-its-not-a), he framed scale as something the player should **feel**, produced by the environment and the giant machines occupying it. The official [Epic Games description](https://store.epicgames.com/p/gen-atlas-ff6272) similarly emphasizes vast plains, deserted facilities, colossal structures and an ever-changing sea rather than map statistics.

That suggests the most useful question is not how large gen ATLAS will be. It is what Ueda intends to do with all that space.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The protagonist of gen ATLAS looks across a flooded landscape toward immense ruined machinery.

contentBlocks.heading: The open world is important because Ueda has always used space differently
contentBlocks.text:
Modern open worlds are often discussed in terms of density. How many activities fit between two points? How quickly does the game reward a detour? How efficiently can a map communicate everything available to the player?

Ueda’s work has often operated from the opposite instinct. **Shadow of the Colossus** is memorable partly because the journey between colossi is allowed to remain a journey. The Forbidden Lands are not constantly interrupting the player with side activities. Distance creates anticipation. Emptiness makes architecture feel larger. Repetition of travel turns Agro from a mount into company.

That history makes Ueda’s confirmation that gen ATLAS is genuinely open world more consequential than the label itself. He told Game Informer that the game is his largest, but immediately redirected the conversation away from measurable area and toward the *sense* of scale. The desert shown so far is also not the whole environment; he confirmed that [other biomes are planned](https://gameinformer.com/interview/2026/06/09/fumito-ueda-discusses-gen-atlas-details-wall-e-inspiration-and-why-its-not-a).

The tension is obvious. Open-world design usually pressures developers to make empty space justify itself. Ueda’s previous games often make emptiness the justification.

If gen ATLAS preserves that philosophy, its world may be less interested in keeping us continuously occupied than in controlling what distance, silence and visibility do to our perception. That would put it in conversation with games such as [Elden Ring’s open-world design](story:elden-ring-open-world-design-legacy), where discovery is powerful precisely because the world does not reduce every destination to an explicit checklist.

contentBlocks.heading: The giant robot is not simply Ueda’s next companion
contentBlocks.text:
It is tempting to draw a clean line through Ueda’s companions: Yorda in ICO, Agro in Shadow of the Colossus, Trico in The Last Guardian, and now the robot head in gen ATLAS. Ueda himself recognizes that lineage, but the new machine appears to complicate it.

According to Ueda, the robot head can operate as **transportation, navigator, tool and partner**. The player can enter it, move with it and connect it to different robot bodies. Those connections can open new possibilities for navigation, combat and puzzles. He has also confirmed that the machine can be tinkered with and upgraded.

That is a meaningful change in design role. Yorda is someone you protect and cooperate with. Agro is transportation, but also becomes emotionally significant through the amount of time spent together. Trico is a companion whose enormous body is simultaneously a character and a traversal system. gen ATLAS appears to compress all of those categories into a single mechanical relationship.

The machine is not merely beside the player. It may determine **what the player is physically capable of doing in the world**.

That makes the recurring Ueda fascination with companionship more systemic than before. A relationship can potentially be expressed through where the machine takes you, which body it inhabits, how it changes, what it helps you reach and how dependent the player becomes on it. If the design works, attachment would not need to arrive only through cutscenes or dialogue. It could accumulate through use.
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A mechanical body travels high above the landscape in gen ATLAS.
contentBlocks.caption: Official gen ATLAS screenshot showing the scale and mobility of its machinery. Credit: genDESIGN / Epic Games.

contentBlocks.heading: Scale is becoming a mechanic instead of only an emotion
contentBlocks.text:
Shadow of the Colossus made scale tactile. A colossus was not impressive because a cutscene told us it was enormous; the player had to climb fur, hold on through violent movement and search across a body that functioned like terrain.

gen ATLAS seems interested in a related idea from another direction. Epic’s official description says the colossal robot’s power will open routes to locations that were previously inaccessible and change the player’s conception of the world. Ueda’s explanation goes further: attaching the robot head to bodies is meant to alter navigation as well as combat and puzzle solving.

That wording is important. The giant machine is not just a spectacular object placed inside the environment. It can change **how the environment is read**.

A cliff that is impossible for the protagonist may become trivial when the robot is available. A distant structure can shift from scenery into destination. A body that initially looks like environmental debris may later become infrastructure. The player’s understanding of scale can therefore evolve alongside their mechanical capabilities.

That is a more interesting use of an enormous open world than simply giving the player faster transportation. The design possibility is that gen ATLAS can repeatedly make familiar spaces feel different by changing the scale at which the player interacts with them.
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The gen ATLAS protagonist stands beside massive damaged machinery in a rocky environment.
contentBlocks.caption: Official gen ATLAS screenshot. Machinery is presented less like a vehicle selection screen and more like part of the physical landscape. Credit: genDESIGN / Epic Games.

contentBlocks.heading: The gun matters less than the freedom Ueda is attaching to it
contentBlocks.text:
The firearm shown in the reveal footage generated an understandable reaction because it is visually foreign to Ueda’s previous protagonists. But treating gen ATLAS as Ueda suddenly making a shooter would be reading the most familiar object in the trailer as the whole game.

Ueda has explicitly rejected that interpretation. In both Game Informer’s interview and a separate [GameSpot conversation](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/fumito-ueda-gen-atlas-interview/), he described shooting as one option for overcoming particular obstacles rather than the central progression loop. He told Game Informer that the player should not expect a system where using the gun more, killing more enemies or accumulating more combat output automatically produces higher rewards.

That distinction fits the larger design picture. If robot bodies, environmental traversal, puzzles and weapons are all tools for progression, gen ATLAS may be built around selecting an appropriate relationship with an obstacle rather than solving every obstacle through combat.

The gun is therefore interesting precisely because it is ordinary. It gives the player one immediately understandable verb inside a world whose larger systems remain unfamiliar. The real question is how often the game encourages us to ignore that obvious verb for a stranger solution.
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The gen ATLAS protagonist aims a futuristic weapon across a wide body of water.
contentBlocks.caption: Official gen ATLAS screenshot. Ueda has stressed that the game includes shooting without being designed as a shooter. Credit: genDESIGN / Epic Games.

contentBlocks.heading: gen ATLAS may communicate more without explaining everything
contentBlocks.text:
Another apparent contradiction sits at the center of the project. Ueda says gen ATLAS will feature **more communication and more on-screen text** than his previous games, yet his approach to writing remains deliberately incomplete.

He described the structure of his scripts to Game Informer through the analogy of haiku: establish a strong opening and ending, build episodes between them, and leave space for the audience to interpret what connects those moments. In gen ATLAS, the science-fiction setting gives him a believable reason to preserve conversations through logs and text, so the player can receive more explicit communication without necessarily receiving a more explicit explanation of the world.

That difference matters. Mystery is not the same thing as withholding all information.

A world can tell the player how a machine works while refusing to tell them why the civilization that built it disappeared. A robot can communicate with the protagonist while its motives remain difficult to read. A log can document an event without resolving its meaning.

If gen ATLAS succeeds at that balance, it could become Ueda’s most verbally communicative game while remaining structurally committed to interpretation.

contentBlocks.heading: The project started with giant robots, not with an open-world checklist
contentBlocks.text:
That is another reason the project does not read like genDESIGN chasing a market category. Ueda has said formal design work began around 2020 after years of prototyping, and he told GameSpot that the project started with **giant robots at its core** before the team gradually built the surrounding science-fiction world.

In Game Informer’s interview, he connected that interest to the robot media he grew up with in Japan, while also naming Giant Robo and WALL-E among works that left an impression on him. At the same time, he emphasized that his own approach is grounded in weight, movement and relationships that feel believable within their worlds.

That combination helps explain why the machinery shown so far looks weathered, awkward and physical rather than sleek. The robot head does not resemble a frictionless superhero suit waiting to be equipped. Its size appears to create problems as often as it solves them.

This is where gen ATLAS could preserve one of Ueda’s most important qualities: **friction**. Trico is memorable partly because it is not a perfectly obedient traversal mechanic. Colossi resist the player physically. Agro has momentum. Architecture has weight.

A modular giant robot could easily become a conventional upgrade tree with increasingly efficient movement. The more interesting possibility is that every increase in capability also changes the player’s relationship with weight, distance and control.

contentBlocks.heading: The real risk is whether an Ueda open world can resist becoming ordinary
contentBlocks.text:
All of this is still interpretation based on limited footage and unusually revealing interviews. We do not know the density of activities, how progression is structured, how often combat occurs, how the robot upgrades work, or how freely the player can move between biomes. The [PlayStation listing](https://www.playstation.com/en-ca/games/gen-atlas/) still gives no release date.

And that uncertainty is important, because making an open world creates pressures that Ueda’s earlier games did not have to solve at this scale.

A large world needs reasons to travel through it. Progression has to remain legible. Repetition becomes easier to notice. Systems that are fascinating for six hours can become routine across thirty. The larger the map becomes, the harder it is to make every ruin feel intentional.

That is why gen ATLAS is compelling to analyze before release. Its ambition is not simply technological. It is philosophical.

Can a creator known for restraint build an open world without filling every silence? Can a companion remain emotionally ambiguous when it is also transportation and equipment? Can enormous machines preserve their sense of scale after the player learns to operate them? Can additional dialogue coexist with mystery? Can a gun sit inside Ueda’s design vocabulary without reorganizing the entire game around combat?

Those are not questions a trailer can answer. But they are much more interesting than asking whether gen ATLAS is merely bigger than Shadow of the Colossus.

quickRead: gen ATLAS is Fumito Ueda’s first confirmed open-world game and the largest world he has built.
The giant robot head can function as transportation, navigator, tool and companion, and can connect to other robot bodies.
Ueda says shooting is only one way to overcome obstacles and has explicitly rejected describing the game as a shooter.
The project appears to extend Ueda’s recurring ideas about scale, companionship, silence and interpretation into open-world systems.
conclusion:
The most promising thing about gen ATLAS is not that Fumito Ueda finally has the technology, publisher or production scale to make something enormous. It is that the game appears to be asking what happens when his smallest design obsessions are given more room.

A giant robot can be a companion, but also a vehicle. Empty space can create loneliness, but also navigation. Scale can inspire awe, but also determine which routes exist. More dialogue can clarify a relationship without clarifying a world.

That is why gen ATLAS currently looks less like a departure from Ueda’s past than a difficult expansion of it. The machinery, firearms and open-world structure are new vocabulary. The underlying questions are familiar.

If the final game can make those ideas reinforce one another instead of becoming separate systems competing for attention, gen ATLAS will not need to imitate ICO, Shadow of the Colossus or The Last Guardian to feel unmistakably like a Fumito Ueda game.
conclusionHeading: Bigger is the least interesting thing about gen ATLAS
